To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the phonetics of words is more complex than previously thought; 2) the phonetics is not entirely predictable from phonological structure and context; 3) the phonetics does not always conform to a simple categorical pattern; 4) phonetic variation is not random, but is systematic and can be described by probabilistic rules; and 5) the variation is not random with respect to the lexicon, but is word specific and systematic.
1. The phonetic realization of a word is affected by its neighbors in a sentence, in the same way as the phonetic realization of an individual segment is affected by its phonetic context.
1. Word-specific phonetic detail is pervasive, even in fluent speakers of English.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the relationship between phonological and phonetic representations, and with the nature of lexical phonetic representations.
the cognitive representations of words and their relation to the phonetic details of their realization, and the relation of these representations to sociostylistsic variation.
the phonetic implementation of lexical items.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there are two types of phonetic variation: (a) systematic phonetic variation in which the phonetic detail is predictable from the phonological structure of the lexemes involved, and (b) idiosyncratic phonetic variation, in which the phonetics of the words are not predictable from the phonology.
there is evidence of word specific phonetics, but it is not yet clear how it is to be explained in a formal model.
the phonetic implementation of words is not fully modular and feedforward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found that there are systematic differences in the phonetics of words which do not map onto categorical differences, and we have found that some of the phonetic variation in speech is not due to sociostylistsic register.
the phonetics of words is not categorical.

the phonetics of speech is a highly structured, modular, and feed forward process, but that the modular feed forward nature of the process has been over emphasized, and the role of the phonetics of the lexicon has been under emphasized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phonetic implementation can be highly variable even within a single language.
phonological representations do not determine phonetic implementation.
the word-specific phonetics we have identified in the data is a robust, systematic effect.
